modes.cue_notes: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Arms rest alongside the body or on the belly. Allow the natural lumbar curve to be present. Let the weight of the body fully release into the floor. This is a neutral spine position — not a stretch, but a resting integration pose.

source: Traditional yin yoga; see Paul Grilley, Bernie Clark, Sarah Powers
notes: Used as a neutral resting position between poses, especially after backbends, hip openers, or inversions. Allows the spine and connective tissues to decompress and integrate.

breathing_cues.entering: As you bend the knees and place the feet, exhale audibly through the mouth to signal the nervous system to downshift.
breathing_cues.holding: Let the breath drop into the belly rather than the chest — feel the lower back gently pressing into the floor on each inhale and softening away on each exhale. The psoas begins to melt with each breath cycle.
breathing_cues.exiting: Take one full inhale before you move, and let the exhale initiate the transition so you stay connected to ease.

modifications.name: Feet wider than hips
modifications.description: Allow feet to be wider than hip-width so the knees can lean against each other, reducing any gripping in the inner thighs and encouraging deeper psoas release.

modifications.name: Hands on belly
modifications.description: Rest both hands on the lower belly to provide biofeedback for diaphragmatic breathing and deepen somatic awareness of the psoas releasing with each exhale.

modifications.name: Blanket under sacrum
modifications.description: Place a thin folded blanket under the sacrum to provide a mild supported tilt for students with significant lumbar tension.

modifications.name: Eyes covered
modifications.description: Use an eye pillow or fold of blanket over the eyes to reduce visual stimulation and encourage a deeper inward parasympathetic shift.

emotional_release_potential.notes: The psoas — the 'muscle of the soul' — holds fear and survival tension. As it passively lengthens in constructive rest, chronic bracing patterns may surface as emotion or trembling. Meet this with breath and stillness.
This pose directly deactivates the fight-flight posture. Students with trauma histories may find the supported neutrality of this shape profoundly disarming — allow extra time and spacious cueing.
